newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BASS UNIT SAYS TAX LAWS THREATEN S.AFRICA GAMING.
newsitem.headline: BASS UNIT SAYS TAX LAWS THREATEN S.AFRICA GAMING.

text.p: Bass Leisure and Southern Sun on Thursday officially launched their new recreational gaming company Monyaka but warned that South Africa's richest province Gauteng could lose out if tax laws weren't revised.
The Southern Sun Group is a subsidiary of South African Breweries and Bass Leisure is a subsidiary of British brewery group Bass Plc .

The remaining two partners in the 250 million rand gaming machine venture are black business organisations National African Federated Chamber of Commerce (Nafcoc) and the Foundation for African and Business Consumer Services (Fabcos).
Emphasising the benefits South Africa stood to win from Monyaka Gaming Machine Supply -- a Sotho word meaning enjoyment -- Roger Withers, director of Bass Leisure South Africa said:
"The investment will have a considerable impact right across the country. Within the next 18 months there will be 90 mln rand invested in the project. There will be 500 direct jobs.

"But there is a small cloud on the horizon. Here in Gauteng we have been discussing vigorously with the authorities the level of taxation. If the level of taxation is too high then none of these things I've said to you is possible."
The joint venture partners said in a statement that the gaming industry had the potential to deliver nationally between 600 and 800 million rand per year in tax revenues.
They added that Gauteng's tax proposal of almost 40 percent of the gross machine income before corporate tax was "double the maximum percentage which a viable industry could sustain".
The Monyaka venture plans to manufacture and distribute gaming machines throughout South Africa by early 1997.

"What we announce today is the end result of a long process of negotiation and learning and it is just the beginning of a very promising and fruitful venture between four parties whose combined forces have the potential to build a very strong foundation for our industry in South Africa," Withers said.

Sam Buthelezi, chairman of Fabcos Gauteng, said that by putting gaming machines in township taverns and shebeens (informal drinking houses) throughout South Africa, Monyaka would be creating vast opportunities for the previously economically disenfranchsied to earn an income.
"Black people will then be in a position where they can too start making money and learn how to pay taxes. This is a success story," Buthelezi said.
Bass Leisure holds a 40 percent stake in Monyaka, Southern Sun 30 percent and Nafcoc and Fabcos each 15 percent.

The gaming machine deal is to be funded by a mixture of equity and debt, Bass leisure's Withers said, adding that much of the debt would have to be raised in South Africa due to the rand's weakness against most foreign currencies.

He said that the Monyaka partners remained hopeful that the manufacturing plant would be in the Free State, but that lately there had been concerns the plant would not be open by the scheduled date early next year.

Ron Stringfellow, group managing director of Southern Sun, which operates and is applying for casino licences, denied that participating in a recreational or soft gaming venture was competing against Southern Sun's other business interests.

He said that while both gaming sectors competed for disposable income, recreational gaming offered entertainment and not substantial prizes and was therefore targeting a market that sought amusement at any venue.
